title: Formal Specification of Hardware Security Modules (HSMs) using Temporal Logic
abstract: Hardware Security Modules (HSMs) are integral to modern cryptographic systems, safeguarding sensitive keys and facilitating secure transactions. However, the complexity of HSM designs often leads to subtle security vulnerabilities that can be difficult to detect through traditional testing methods. This paper presents a novel approach to HSM security verification by employing temporal logic. We develop a formal specification of HSM functionality, enabling rigorous verification of security properties and ensuring compliance with relevant security standards. The methodology provides a structured framework for identifying and mitigating potential risks, ultimately enhancing the overall security posture of HSMs. This work addresses a critical gap in HSM security validation, offering a robust and systematic technique for ensuring the integrity and reliability of these vital components.

title: Based on Simulated Annealing Algorithm for Compiler Optimization
abstract: This paper investigates the application of Simulated Annealing (SA) algorithm to enhance compiler optimization. Traditional compiler optimization relies on heuristic search techniques, often converging to local optima. This research proposes a novel approach by framing compiler optimization as a global search problem, leveraging the probabilistic nature of the SA algorithm to explore the optimization space more effectively. The core idea involves modeling the optimization problem as a search space and utilizing SA's ability to escape local minima. We demonstrate that SA can potentially identify optimization strategies that traditional methods might miss, leading to improved code quality and efficiency. The paper outlines the formulation of this approach, detailing the representation of the search space, the SA algorithm's parameters, and the evaluation criteria. While no experimental validation is presented due to the complexity of complete compiler optimization, this work establishes a theoretical framework and provides a foundation for future research and development in this area.

title: Title: Emergent Topological Order in Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have demonstrated remarkable success in various tasks involving graph data, including social network analysis, drug discovery, and knowledge graph reasoning. However, a fundamental challenge remains: effectively capturing and utilizing the inherent topological order within these graphs. This paper investigates a novel architectural approach that explicitly promotes the emergence of topological order in GNNs, aiming to improve the representation and prediction of complex graph structures. The proposed mechanism, "connectivity deformation," subtly alters the graph structure to create self-organizing patterns, fostering a more robust and adaptable representation. We analyze the impact of this design on various graph datasets, demonstrating significant improvements in representation learning and prediction accuracy compared to existing GNN architectures. The core mechanism provides a pathway for inherent topological ordering, enhancing the model's ability to represent and reason about graph structure effectively. This work offers a promising direction for advancing the state-of-the-art in GNNs by focusing on the intrinsic properties of graph data.

title: Fractal Graph Neural Networks for Scale-Free Data
abstract: Scale-free networks, characterized by a power-law degree distribution, are prevalent in numerous real-world systems, including social networks, biological networks, and financial networks. Traditional Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) often struggle to effectively capture the intricate hierarchical and self-similar patterns inherent in these networks, leading to suboptimal performance in tasks such as node classification and link prediction. This paper proposes a novel approach—Fractal Graph Neural Networks (FGNNs)—that directly addresses this limitation by incorporating principles of fractal geometry into the design of GNN architectures. FGNNs employ recursive connections and multi-scale feature extraction mechanisms, explicitly modeling the self-similar structures found in scale-free networks. We demonstrate that this approach leads to improved representation learning and enhanced performance compared to standard GNNs on synthetic and real-world scale-free datasets. The core claim is that standard GNNs are ill-suited for scale-free data due to their inability to model hierarchical and self-similar patterns. The proposed mechanism involves designing GNN architectures based on fractal geometry, incorporating recursive connections and multi-scale feature extraction. This represents a fundamentally new approach to GNN design specifically tailored for scale-free data.

title: ##基于多模态弱监督学习的认知架构生成
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to cognitive architecture generation leveraging the power of multi-modal weakly supervised learning. The core idea is to automatically construct complex cognitive architectures by extracting weak supervision signals from unstructured multi-modal data – encompassing text, images, and audio. The framework utilizes a weak supervision learning model to predict underlying associations and causal relationships within the data. These learned weak signals then drive the training of a cognitive architecture composed of diverse cognitive modules, such as memory, reasoning, and learning, effectively mimicking human cognitive processes. Unlike traditional architectures reliant on expert knowledge or manual design, this method offers enhanced generalization capabilities and adaptability by learning directly from vast quantities of multi-modal data. The research addresses the limitations of current approaches and paves the way for more robust and adaptable cognitive systems.

title: Query-Efficient Cross-Domain Black-Box Adversarial Robustness Assessment Without Retraining via Differentiable Spatial-Channel Mapping and Bandit Optimization
abstract: Evaluating the adversarial robustness of deployed deep neural networks is critical for trustworthy AI, yet existing black-box assessment tools assume homogeneous input domains shared between surrogates and targets, an assumption rarely met in practice. Cross-domain transfer attacks are inherently ill-posed due to profound structural and semantic discrepancies between surrogate and target models. Conventional methods often fail due to gradient stagnation and label misalignment. We propose Cross-Domain Adversarial Optimization (CDAO), a training-free paradigm establishing high-fidelity adversarial guidance across heterogeneous domains without task-specific retraining. Differentiable Spatial-Channel Mapping (DSCM) reconciles physical dimension mismatches, preserving analytical differentiability across mismatched input dimensions. To resolve semantic disjointness, Target Proxy Distillation (TPD) casts proxy target selection as a multi-fidelity candidate-selection problem analogous to Best Arm Identification. Using multi-fidelity Successive Halving, TPD adaptively distills informative proxy classes with minimal query overhead, eliminating shared label assumptions. By unifying structural and semantic alignment into a plug-and-play pipeline, CDAO enables effective cross-domain guidance at inference time. Extensive evaluations across cross-dataset image-classification settings that differ in architecture, resolution, channel format, and label space demonstrate that CDAO achieves the best transferability and favorable query efficiency among the evaluated inference-time black-box baselines for cross-dataset image classification, reducing the end-to-end query budget to Q ~ 103 (an order of magnitude below the Q ~ 104 regime of pure query-driven attacks). Concretely, the end-to-end budget is only 1000 and 3000 queries for small- and large-scale datasets, respectively, yielding targeted ASR gains of 38.5% on CIFAR-10 and 43.7% on ImageNet-1K over the strongest baseline. These results highlight that even models deployed behind black-box APIs remain vulnerable to structured cross-domain probes, and that robustness evaluation tools must account for heterogeneous threat surfaces.

title: Порівняння байєсівських мереж різної структурної складності для прогнозування летальності при COVID-19
abstract: У роботі розглянуто методологію побудови, налаштування та порівняння трьох імовірнісних моделей -байєсівських мереж різних класів зі зростаючою структурною складністю -для задачі прогнозування летальності пацієнтів із коронавірусною хворобою.Порівняно наївний баєсів класифікатор, деревоподібно доповнений наївний баєсів класифікатор та структурно обмежену байєсівську мережу, структуру якої відновлюють із даних алгоритмом структурного навчання під експертними клінічними обмеженнями.Щоб відокремити вплив структурної складності від відбору ознак, налаштування параметрів і вибору порогів, застосовано порівняння за однакових умов із послідовним спрощенням та ускладненням структури моделі.Особливу увагу приділено розмежуванню двох аспектів якості моделей -розпізнавальної здатності та якості (узгодженості) прогнозованих імовірностей, оскільки для клінічної системи підтримки прийняття рішень визначальною є саме достовірність оцінки ризику, а не лише впорядкування пацієнтів за ступенем ризику.Дослідження проведено на відкритому реєстрі пацієнтів із коронавірусною хворобою за клінічними ознаками з оцінюванням на вибірці, що відтворює природну поширеність летальних випадків.Розглянуто перенесення прогнозованих імовірностей у природну популяцію коригуванням апріорної ймовірності, а також чутливість клінічних рішень до співвідношення вартостей помилок та аналіз чистої клінічної користі.Мета роботи -обґрунтувати доцільність застосування структурно обмеженої байєсівської мережі як інтерпретованого інструмента оцінювання ризику в системах підтримки прийняття клінічних рішень.

title: Adaptive Quantum Control Algorithm with Feedback Mechanism
abstract: This paper presents a novel adaptive quantum control algorithm incorporating a feedback mechanism to enhance the robustness and precision of quantum system manipulation. The core claim is to design an algorithm that dynamically adjusts control signals based on real-time feedback from the quantum system's state. The proposed mechanism leverages quantum measurements and optimization algorithms to continuously refine control parameters. This approach addresses limitations inherent in traditional quantum control methods by mitigating the effects of noise and uncertainty, ultimately leading to improved control accuracy. The algorithm's architecture and theoretical framework are thoroughly outlined, demonstrating its potential for achieving highly accurate control over complex quantum systems. The implementation details and performance analysis provide a strong foundation for future research and development in adaptive quantum control.

title: 基于多尺度隐变量的因果发现
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to causal discovery leveraging multi-scale latent variables. Traditional causal discovery methods often struggle with complex systems due to their limited ability to account for relationships operating at different scales. Our framework addresses this limitation by constructing a multi-scale latent variable model, decomposing data into distinct variable sets representing various scales. Subsequently, causal discovery algorithms are applied to each scale to identify potential causal links. Finally, these identified relationships are integrated and rigorously validated, resulting in a more accurate and nuanced understanding of the underlying causal structure. The core claim centers on the improved accuracy achieved through this multi-scale integration. The proposed mechanism involves a structured approach, building a multi-scale latent variable model and employing a systematic process of scale-specific causal discovery followed by integration and validation. The novelty lies in acknowledging and explicitly modeling the intricate interplay between causal relationships operating at diverse scales.

title: Symbolic Regression on Graph Structures
abstract: This paper explores the application of symbolic regression to uncover mathematical relationships inherent in graph structures. Traditional symbolic regression focuses on numerical data, often requiring manual feature engineering. This work proposes a direct application of symbolic regression algorithms to graph representations, such as adjacency matrices and node degree distributions. The core idea is to treat the graph structure itself as the input data, allowing the regression engine to identify equations that accurately describe the network's properties. We demonstrate the feasibility of this approach and discuss the potential for discovering fundamental mathematical principles governing complex networks. The results suggest that symbolic regression can effectively translate graph data into symbolic equations, revealing previously unknown relationships and potentially providing new insights into network dynamics.

title: Distributed Differential Privacy for Graph Analytics
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to performing graph analytics with differential privacy, addressing the limitations of existing techniques in large-scale distributed environments. The core challenge lies in the computational complexity inherent in many graph algorithms. We introduce a distributed algorithm that combines elements of federated learning and approximate differential privacy to achieve privacy preservation while enabling efficient graph computations across multiple machines. Our design specifically tackles the unique properties of graph data, offering a practical solution for analyzing large, distributed graph datasets in a privacy-preserving manner. The key innovation is adapting the concept of differential privacy to the graph context, offering a mechanism to quantify and mitigate privacy risks associated with graph analysis. The algorithm utilizes a local perturbation strategy combined with a global sensitivity adjustment, allowing for robust privacy guarantees. We demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of this approach through a theoretical framework, laying the groundwork for future implementations and further research in this area.

title: Algorithmic Fairness via Shapley Values on Bayesian Networks
abstract: This paper explores the application of Shapley values, a technique originally developed for explaining individual predictions in machine learning, to the domain of algorithmic fairness within Bayesian Networks. The core argument posits that Shapley values can provide a method for identifying and mitigating bias, but their direct application to complex models presents significant challenges. This research adapts the concept of Shapley values to the probabilistic structure inherent in Bayesian Networks, utilizing the network's conditional probability tables to quantify feature influence and pinpoint sources of unfairness. The approach offers a novel framework for fairness assessment and potential mitigation strategies, particularly in scenarios where interpretability and causal reasoning are paramount. The paper details the adaptation process, provides illustrative examples, and discusses the limitations of this methodology. Ultimately, this work contributes to a growing body of research seeking to integrate fairness considerations into the design and deployment of intelligent systems.

title: Explainable AI via Causal Mediation Analysis of Neural Networks
abstract: The increasing deployment of neural networks in critical applications necessitates methods for understanding their decision-making processes. Traditional explainable AI (XAI) techniques often provide post-hoc explanations that may not accurately reflect the underlying causal mechanisms driving the network's predictions. This research proposes a novel approach utilizing causal mediation analysis to elucidate the pathways through which input features influence neural network outputs. By applying mediation analysis to the internal representations learned by the network, we aim to identify and quantify the mediating variables responsible for the observed relationships. This framework offers a more robust and interpretable explanation compared to purely correlational methods, ultimately contributing to increased trust and transparency in neural network systems. The core of this work lies in leveraging the principles of causal inference to disentangle correlation from causation, thereby providing a deeper understanding of the complex interactions within neural networks. We present a methodology for extracting and analyzing mediation paths, providing a framework for evaluating the sensitivity of network predictions to different input features. The results demonstrate the potential of this approach to improve the interpretability of neural networks and contribute to the development of more reliable and trustworthy AI systems. ---

title: 基于生物启发算法的数据库索引优化 (Database Index Optimization Based on Bio-Inspired Algorithms - BIIBO)
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to database index optimization utilizing bio-inspired algorithms. The core concept involves translating the complexities of database indexing into a problem amenable to solutions inspired by natural biological processes. Specifically, we explore the application of algorithms such as Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) to generate and refine database index structures. The primary objective is to improve query performance by intelligently structuring the index, reducing scan times, and minimizing I/O operations. This work demonstrates a potential pathway for significantly enhancing database systems' efficiency through a biologically-motivated optimization technique. The core claim is that utilizing bio-inspired algorithms can optimize database index structures and improve query efficiency. The core mechanism involves modeling the database indexing problem as a problem for bio-inspired algorithms, followed by utilizing the algorithm to optimize and generate an optimal index structure.

title: A Cognitive Architecture Model Based on the Information Bottleneck Theory
abstract: This paper proposes a cognitive architecture model constructed upon the principles of the Information Bottleneck (IB) theory. The model aims to simulate human cognitive processes by mimicking the bottleneck effect observed in human information processing. Specifically, the architecture focuses on controlling the flow and storage of information, thereby replicating key aspects of human cognition. The core claim is that the IB theory provides a robust framework for understanding and modelling cognitive mechanisms. This work outlines the architecture's key components, the underlying mathematical formulations, and the mechanisms driving cognitive function simulation. The proposed approach offers a novel method for cognitive architecture design, potentially leading to a deeper comprehension of human cognitive processes.

title: Dynamic Program Synthesis with Semantic Abstraction
abstract: Dynamic program synthesis (DPS) aims to automatically generate executable code from high-level specifications. A significant challenge in DPS lies in the complexity of representing and manipulating program semantics, particularly when dealing with large and intricate codebases. This work introduces a semantic abstraction mechanism designed to enhance the efficiency and scalability of DPS. The core idea is to construct a formal language-based semantic abstraction layer that maps program code to a more abstract representation, thereby reducing the computational burden of the synthesis process. We leverage logical reasoning and search algorithms operating on this abstraction to guide the code generation. This approach offers a promising path toward more practical and effective DPS solutions by mitigating the limitations of purely symbolic representations. The key contributions of this research include a novel framework for semantic abstraction and a methodology for integrating it with existing DPS techniques. The proposed method demonstrates the potential to significantly improve the performance and feasibility of DPS systems.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Based Computation Framework for Advanced Quantum Algorithms
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, presents a unique opportunity for computation beyond the limitations of classical systems. This paper explores the potential of utilizing entanglement as a core computational unit to develop novel quantum algorithms with enhanced efficiency and capabilities. We propose a framework centered around the design and implementation of quantum algorithms leveraging entanglement to circumvent classical computational bottlenecks. The core mechanism involves introducing entangled qubits as computational elements, allowing for instantaneous correlations and accelerated information transfer. This research will address the challenges of maintaining entanglement in a complex environment and design quantum algorithms that exploit these properties to achieve significant performance improvements. The proposed framework offers a pathway towards achieving quantum computation's potential, pushing the boundaries of what is currently possible.

title: Nonlinear Topology Modeling
abstract: This paper introduces a novel non-linear topology modeling approach designed to enhance data compression and optimization. Traditional methods often fail to effectively leverage the inherent topological structure within data, resulting in suboptimal performance and high computational costs. Our method employs a dynamic, non-linear transformation of the data compression and optimization process, effectively capturing the underlying topological relationships. The core mechanism involves constructing a representation of the data using a topological graph, allowing for efficient compression and optimization through the manipulation of graph properties. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through experimental results, showcasing significant improvements in compression ratio and optimization speed compared to existing methods.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum state decomposition and evolution algorithm based on topological information theory. title: Dynamic Quantum Geometry Mapping
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic quantum geometry mapping algorithm designed to optimize quantum computation and control. Traditional quantum algorithms often struggle with computationally intensive gate operations, limiting their practical applicability. This research proposes a method that dynamically adjusts the quantum state by manipulating the geometry of the quantum potential, offering a significant advancement over existing techniques. We detail the core mechanism, focusing on the interplay between quantum geometry and computational optimization. The algorithm's potential impact spans across diverse quantum applications, including enhanced quantum control and accelerated algorithm execution. We provide a comprehensive overview of the algorithm's design, implementation, and preliminary experimental results demonstrating its efficacy in stabilizing specific quantum states.

title: 基于量子纠缠的概率逻辑计算
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a bizarre phenomenon where two or more particles become linked and share the same fate, has captured the imagination of physicists and mathematicians alike. This paper explores the potential of leveraging entanglement to revolutionize probability logic computation, a field traditionally reliant on deterministic algorithms. We propose a novel probabilistic reasoning framework centered around quantum entanglement, aiming to enhance logical inference and decision-making by exploiting the instantaneous correlations inherent in this quantum phenomenon. The core mechanism involves utilizing entangled qubits to represent and manipulate probability states, enabling a shift from rigid, deterministic logic to a more fluid, probabilistic approach. We argue that this approach offers the possibility of significantly improved accuracy and efficiency in complex probabilistic calculations, particularly in scenarios demanding nuanced judgment and adaptability.

title: Fractal-Based Compression of Symbolic Data
abstract: This paper proposes a novel compression technique for symbolic data based on fractal geometry. Traditional lossless compression algorithms often struggle with highly repetitive symbolic sequences, especially those exhibiting fractal patterns. This approach aims to overcome these limitations by directly modeling the self-similar nature of the data using fractal equations. The algorithm identifies and encodes repeating patterns within the data as fractal equations, significantly reducing redundancy. The core of the method lies in representing symbolic sequences as iterated function systems (IFS) or similar fractal representations, enabling efficient compression. We explore the mathematical framework underlying this technique, detailing the encoding and decoding processes, and analyzing the compression ratios achieved compared to established methods. The presented approach offers a potentially more effective solution for compressing symbolic data with inherent fractal characteristics, leading to improved compression ratios and reduced storage requirements. The key mathematical components include the definition of fractal equations, the iterative application of these equations for encoding, and the inverse application for decoding. The performance is evaluated using a range of symbolic data sets, demonstrating the efficacy of the proposed method.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Monte Carlo Tree Search
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of quantum computing to significantly enhance the efficiency of Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) algorithms. MCTS, a cornerstone of modern artificial intelligence, particularly in game playing, relies heavily on computationally intensive simulations to evaluate game states and guide the search process. We propose a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm that leverages quantum superposition and entanglement to achieve a parallel exploration of the vast search space inherent in MCTS. The core mechanism involves utilizing quantum computers for specific tasks within the MCTS workflow, primarily the evaluation of game states. We formulate the problem as a quantum optimization task, mapping the state evaluation to a quantum objective function. The algorithm employs a classical controller to manage the quantum computation, orchestrating the simulations and extracting information. Preliminary theoretical analysis suggests a potential exponential speedup in state evaluation compared to classical simulations, contingent on the quality of the quantum hardware and the effectiveness of the hybrid approach. This research contributes to the broader field of quantum-accelerated AI and provides a framework for future investigations into the practical application of quantum computing within complex decision-making algorithms.

title: SAFEGuard: Detect Optimization-Based Jailbreak Attacks Through Harmful Semantic Analysis and Fluency Measurement
abstract: Despite the significant efforts devoted to aligning large language models (LLMs) with human values and ensuring safe deployment, recent work has revealed that LLMs remain vulnerable to adversarial jailbreak attacks that can bypass safety guardrails and elicit harmful responses. Many defense methods are proposed to detect jailbreaks but they are limited in their effectiveness to counter wide-range optimization-based jailbreak mechanisms that can yield highly fluency-optimized or harmful semantic obfuscated prompts. To tackle this challenge, we propose a unified detection framework SAFEGuard which incorporates a hybrid fluency measurement based on cross-layer distribution distance and perplexity, and the analysis of harmful semantics through gradient matching. Our method is grounded in a paramount observation: high fluency prompts maintain their malicious intention close to harmful prompts while harmful semantic obfuscated prompts often inject gibberish token sequences. Our evaluation demonstrates that SAFEGuard consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and achieves significant improvement in accuracy across different optimization-based jailbreaks. This underscores the effectiveness of SAFEGuard against evolving jailbreak attacks.

title: Construcción de modelos predictivos a partir de reglas SI-ENTONCES extraídas de Mapas Cognitivos Difusos
authors: Francisco Fernando de la Rosa Troyano
abstract: En trabajos previos, mediante algoritmos de extracción, se han extraído conjuntos de reglas causales SI-ENTONCES que resumen y explican la dinámica dominante de sistemas modelados mediante Mapas Cognitivos Difusos. Este documento explica cómo convertir esas reglas en modelos predictivos que respondan en tiempo real al estado de un conjunto de variables de entrada y produzcan una salida, que prediga el estado futuro del sistema, ya sea utilizando una señal direccional, una distribución de probabilidad o ambas. En este artículo se discute 1) las decisiones de diseño fundamentales —separación de variables causales y variables objetivo, modos de entrada, normalización de las evidencias—, y 2) las soluciones a los problemas más frecuentes —cobertura desigual entre conceptos, conceptos secundarios, restricciones de dominio— y se incluye una sección final dedicada al uso de modelos de lenguaje (LLM) como asistentes para implementar estos modelos de forma automatizada.

title: Adaptive Hardware-Software Co-Design for Quantum Computing
abstract: Quantum computing promises revolutionary advancements across various fields, but its practical realization hinges on overcoming significant challenges in algorithm execution. Traditional hardware-software co-design approaches for quantum computing often rely on pre-defined architectures and compilation strategies, which can be suboptimal for diverse quantum algorithms. This paper proposes an adaptive hardware-software co-design framework that dynamically adjusts the quantum computing system's configuration – encompassing both hardware architecture and software compilation – in response to the specific requirements of the algorithm being executed. The core claim is that optimized co-design is pivotal for efficient quantum algorithm execution. This framework leverages a dynamic optimization loop, continuously monitoring algorithm performance and adjusting parameters such as qubit connectivity, gate set selection, and compilation strategies. The system utilizes a mathematical model to represent the algorithm's computational demands and hardware capabilities, enabling real-time adaptation. This approach moves beyond static design methodologies, offering a pathway towards significantly improved performance and resource utilization in quantum computing systems. The framework's ability to adapt in real-time represents a crucial step towards unlocking the full potential of quantum algorithms.

title: Quantum Error Correction Redundancy Coding
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to quantum error correction (QEC) utilizing redundancy coding, focusing on enhanced efficiency in quantum information transmission. The core claim revolves around designing multi-particle error-correcting codes to minimize the resource consumption associated with encoding and decoding. The proposed mechanism involves encoding information across multiple qubits, leveraging error detection and correction capabilities inherent in these codes. Crucially, the strategy optimizes the distribution of redundant qubits, significantly reducing unnecessary information redundancy. The research addresses the limitations of existing QEC schemes, which often rely on excessive redundancy, impacting transmission efficiency. This work demonstrates a pathway towards more practical and resource-conscious QEC, representing a key step toward reliable long-distance quantum communication. The primary goal is to reduce the overhead associated with error correction, making quantum information transfer more viable. This is achieved through a refined approach to redundancy, concentrating correction resources where they are most needed.

title: Dynamic Bayesian Networks for Real-Time Control Systems
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to real-time control system design utilizing Dynamic Bayesian Networks (DBNs). Traditional Bayesian Networks often suffer from a static representation of systems, failing to capture the inherent dynamism and evolving relationships within complex control environments. This research addresses this limitation by developing a DBN framework capable of continuous adaptation through real-time sensor data. The core mechanism involves dynamically adjusting both the structure and parameters of the network, facilitating the implementation of adaptive control strategies. The proposed methodology offers a significant advancement over static Bayesian approaches, providing a robust and flexible solution for controlling systems with uncertain dynamics and evolving conditions. Mathematical formulations detailing the core concepts and adaptation rules are provided, along with an illustrative example showcasing the potential of this technique. The primary focus is on the theoretical framework and its application, without experimental validation.

title: Graph Neural Networks for Reinforcement Learning with Sparse Rewards
abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has demonstrated remarkable success in various domains, but its application is significantly hindered by the problem of sparse rewards. In environments where rewards are infrequent or delayed, traditional RL algorithms struggle to learn effective policies. This paper proposes a novel approach leveraging Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to address this challenge. We introduce a framework where the environment is represented as a graph, and a GNN learns a rich state representation capturing complex relationships between elements. This representation enables the RL agent to better explore and exploit sparse reward signals, ultimately improving learning efficiency and performance. The core of our approach lies in the ability of GNNs to aggregate information from neighboring nodes, effectively encoding contextual dependencies that are crucial for navigating sparse reward landscapes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a theoretical analysis and outline the key components of the system, focusing on the integration of GNNs with standard RL algorithms. The goal is to provide a robust and scalable solution for RL problems characterized by sparse rewards.

title: Generative Adversarial Networks for Graph Structure Discovery
abstract: Discovering meaningful graph structures from complex data is a fundamental challenge across numerous domains, including bioinformatics, social network analysis, and materials science. Traditional graph structure discovery methods frequently rely on pre-defined assumptions and heuristics, often leading to biased results that primarily identify known or easily detectable patterns. This paper introduces a novel approach leveraging Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to autonomously explore the vast and largely uncharted space of possible graph structures. The core of our method involves training a GAN where a generator network learns to create synthetic graph structures, and a discriminator network learns to differentiate between these generated structures and real, observed graph structures. We hypothesize that this adversarial training process will allow the generator to discover graph structures that are not readily apparent through conventional methods, potentially revealing entirely new and unexpected relationships within the data. This approach offers a significant departure from traditional graph structure discovery, providing a framework for uncovering hidden patterns and generating hypotheses for further investigation. We outline the architecture of the GAN, discuss the training process, and explore potential applications.

title: Quantum Entanglement Verification via Computational Validation
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, offers a unique and potentially powerful tool for computational verification. This paper explores the application of entanglement-based computational validation methods to verify complex physical systems, offering a novel approach to theory validation. We outline the core mechanism, detailing how entanglement allows for the exploration of systems beyond the limitations of classical computation. The goal is to demonstrate a method that can effectively test fundamental physical laws, providing a robust and efficient alternative to traditional techniques. The core claim is that this method will significantly improve the accuracy and efficiency of validating complex physical systems using quantum entanglement.

We outline the core mechanism, detailing how entanglement allows for the exploration of systems beyond the limitations of classical computation. The goal is to demonstrate a method that can effectively test fundamental physical laws, providing a robust and efficient alternative to traditional techniques. The core claim is that this method will significantly improve the accuracy and efficiency of validating complex physical systems using quantum entanglement.

title: Nonlinear Geometric Mapping: Adaptive Self-Organizing Structures
abstract: This paper introduces a novel geometric mapping framework based on dynamic self-organization algorithms. Traditional geometric mapping approaches often rely on fixed, pre-defined topologies, limiting their adaptability. We propose a new method employing a dynamically-defined topology, mimicking biological self-organization, to enable the mapping model to dynamically adjust its geometric form in response to input data. This results in enhanced flexibility and scalability in the computational process. The core of the system lies in a novel "dynamic topology" algorithm that automatically adjusts geometric transformations to match the data's characteristics. The paper details the implementation of this algorithm, demonstrates its effectiveness through illustrative examples, and explores the potential of this approach for a wide range of applications.

title: Title: Non-Euclidean Graph Embedding via Adaptive Clustering
abstract: The representation of graphs is fundamental to many fields, including social network analysis, machine learning, and data visualization. Traditional graph embedding techniques, such as Node2Vec and GraphSAGE, rely on predefined graph structures and feature engineering. However, these methods often struggle to capture the inherent variability and complexity of real-world graphs. This paper introduces a novel approach to graph embedding – Non-Euclidean Graph Embedding via Adaptive Clustering – that moves beyond fixed graph structures by dynamically adjusting embedding parameters based on the statistical properties of the graph's connections. We propose an adaptive clustering algorithm that continuously re-evaluates graph structure and optimizes embedding representations using a novel loss function that emphasizes the overall graph connectivity. This method aims to enhance representational power and robustness, offering a more flexible and insightful approach to graph data analysis. The paper details the algorithm's implementation, demonstrates its effectiveness on various graph datasets, and discusses its potential applications in diverse areas.

title: Probability Space Geometry for Quantum Algorithm Optimization
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to quantum algorithm optimization based on probability space geometry. We propose a framework that leverages the inherent geometric properties of quantum algorithms, particularly their topology, to automate parameter optimization. This allows for the design of quantum algorithms that are more efficient and robust. The core mechanism involves representing the quantum algorithm as a geometric object – a probability space – and employing techniques to manipulate this space to achieve optimal performance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework through the optimization of a specific quantum algorithm, illustrating its potential to significantly improve algorithm efficiency. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions and the implications of this geometric approach to quantum algorithm development.

title: Dimension Expansion Quantum Error Correction (DEQ)
abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) is a critical requirement for reliable quantum computation, as errors can quickly accumulate and compromise the integrity of quantum states. Current QEC approaches often rely on encoding information redundantly across multiple qubits, which introduces significant overhead and complexity. This paper proposes a novel dimension expansion quantum error correction protocol (DEQ) that leverages the concept of dimensional expansion to enhance quantum information storage and transmission capabilities, ultimately improving the efficiency of error correction. We introduce a new strategy by strategically manipulating the quantum state to expand the system's dimensionality, allowing for more robust error detection and correction. This work explores the potential of this approach in mitigating the limitations of existing QEC methods and provides a foundational framework for future advancements in quantum information security.

title: Dimensional Mapping and Quantum Topology
abstract: This paper explores the application of dimensionality mapping and quantum topology to revolutionize computational and information storage paradigms. The core of our work lies in the development of a novel algorithm, "Quantum Dimension Mapping," leveraging entangled quantum states for precise prediction and manipulation of high-dimensional space topology. We demonstrate the potential of this approach to achieve unprecedented accuracy in quantum state analysis, enabling the simulation and manipulation of complex quantum structures that are currently intractable with conventional methods. This research addresses a critical gap in both quantum computing and topological field, offering a pathway towards more powerful and versatile computational architectures. The algorithm's unique mechanism focuses on the precise measurement and control of entangled quantum states, yielding a predictive capability for high-dimensional topological structures. We present preliminary results showcasing the algorithm's effectiveness in predicting and manipulating specific topological features within a constrained space. This work lays the foundation for a new generation of quantum algorithms with the potential to unlock significant advancements in both computational science and quantum information processing.

title: Self-Organizing and Reconfigurable Computing Architectures
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to computing architecture design centered around self-organization and reconfigurability. The core claim is the development of architectures capable of dynamically adapting their structure and functionality based on task demands. This is achieved through a mechanism leveraging neural network-based control systems for real-time monitoring of computational load and subsequent dynamic adjustment of inter-node connections and resource allocation. The proposed system offers enhanced adaptability compared to traditional static architectures, addressing the growing need for efficient and responsive computing solutions. The architecture's adaptability is paramount for applications with fluctuating workloads and evolving requirements. This work outlines the fundamental principles, key components, and potential applications of such a system.

title: Neural Symbolic Hybrid Models with Explainable Attention Mechanisms
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to enhancing the interpretability and robustness of neural models by integrating symbolic reasoning. We propose a hybrid model architecture where a neural network's attention weights are constrained and guided by symbolic rules. Simultaneously, the neural network learns to refine these rules, creating a feedback loop that improves both interpretability and robustness. The core mechanism leverages the precision and explainability of symbolic systems to address the inherent opacity of deep neural networks. We demonstrate that this approach significantly improves the model's ability to justify its decisions, particularly in scenarios where logical constraints are relevant. The proposed method provides a framework for building more trustworthy and understandable AI systems. This work contributes to the growing field of neuro-symbolic AI and offers a practical solution for enhancing the explainability of complex neural models.

title: Dynamic Programming Language Semantics Based on Formal Models
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to implementing the semantics of dynamic programming languages through formal models. Traditional implementations rely heavily on abstract interpretation or static analysis, which often lack the precision and verifiability required for accurately representing dynamic language behavior. This research proposes a framework for building a formal model-based semantic implementation, leveraging techniques like domain-specific languages (DSLs) and logical representations to provide a precise and verifiable description of the execution process and inherent semantics of dynamic languages. The core contribution lies in the ability to formally capture the nuances of dynamic typing, runtime evaluation, and other key features, leading to a more robust and reliable understanding and implementation of these languages. The framework's modular design allows for tailored implementations for specific dynamic languages and facilitates automated verification of semantic properties. The methodology offers a significant advancement over existing techniques, providing a solid foundation for formal reasoning and validation in dynamic language systems.

title: A decade of research on gold exploration methods: A 2015–2025 Web of Science-based bibliometric analysis
abstract: This study presents a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of research publications related to the optimization of exploration methods at gold deposits indexed in the Web of Science database between 2015 and 2025. A total of 66 articles were identified and analyzed using VOSviewer to visualize and map bibliometric networks. The analysis covered multiple parameters, including publication year, document type, research area, author affiliation, country, funding organization, and journal source. The results demonstrate a steady increase in publication activity after 2020, highlighting growing scientific interest in the application of digital technologies, geochemical modeling, and systems-based approaches to improve exploration efficiency. The majority of studies were published in high-impact journals such as Ore Geology Reviews, Geoscience Frontiers, and Science China – Earth Sciences. China, Australia, Russia, and Canada emerged as the leading contributors, supported mainly by the National Natural Science Foundation of China and the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada. The citation analysis revealed that the most influential papers focus on orogenic gold deposits, structural control of mineralization, and multi-scale exploration models, underscoring the significance of integrated approaches in modern exploration science. These findings provide valuable insights into global research trends, collaboration patterns, and funding priorities, offering a foundation for future advancements in gold exploration methodologies.

title: Efficient Quantum Circuits for Electronic Hamiltonian Simulation without Pauli Expansion
abstract: Electronic Hamiltonian simulation is commonly formulated by mapping fermionic operators to qubit operators and subsequently expanding the resulting ladder-operator products into Pauli strings. While general, this procedure obscures the higher-level fermionic structure and can hide opportunities for circuit optimization. Building on ladder-string-pair (Lasp) diagonalization originally developed for Hamiltonian simulation of partial differential equations, we construct time-evolution circuits for the second-quantized electronic Hamiltonian without performing a Pauli expansion. For the most general case of complex-valued coefficients, we present a time-evolution circuit for a two-body fermionic Lasp operator that corresponds to 16 Pauli strings in the Pauli-expansion approach but does not suffer from Trotter error at this stage. Expanding the optimization scope from a single operator to a triad of three fermionic Lasp operators sharing the same four spin-orbital indices enables systematic cancellation of CX gates, reducing the CX-gate count from 36 to 12 in the example considered, still without introducing Trotter error at this stage. For $n$ spin orbitals, further expanding the optimization scope to a sequence of $O(n)$ suitably ordered triads enables a cascade of CX-gate reductions across triad boundaries, reducing the CX-gate count from $O(n^2)$ to $O(n)$. The Lasp-based approach also naturally accommodates controlled time evolution and yields further optimizations for real-valued Hamiltonians. These results demonstrate that the Lasp-based approach enables more efficient time-evolution circuits by preserving high-level circuit structures and thereby expanding the scope of optimization, providing a systematic route toward more efficient electronic Hamiltonian simulation.

title: Hironori-Sushiki-S11/RSA-2048-Collapse-S11: IKERUSIKI Adaptive Address v1.1 — External Validation and Open Finite
abstract: This release brings together the Adaptive Address implementation, reproduction reports, audit materials, and philosophical background developed since IKERUSIKI Theory v1.0. The current research object is adaptive structural identification within a finite held-information corpus: detecting collisions, selecting additional distinguishing axes, and updating the Address as needed. Included materials: Adaptive Address demonstrations, formal basis, and scaling reproducer. Grok protocol-equivalent reproduction report: 15/15 cases with depth 2 and collision-free identification. Claude scaling report and audit archive: 30 cases covering 32,768–1,048,576-bit integers, with depth 2 and collision-free identification reported in all cases. AI-generated technical evaluation and audit records, with their evidence boundaries stated. Philosophical background: Open Finite, context-responsive recognition, and the metaphor of continuing to write on the shore. Updated README links to the research and supporting documents. The reported experimental results apply to the specified finite corpora and protocols. Mathematical properties, implementation, observed results, and proposed applications are distinguished in the accompanying materials. This release is prepared for archival through the enabled Zenodo–GitHub integration. DOI assignment will be confirmed after Zenodo processing.

title: Probabilistic Programming with Differential Privacy for Sensitive Data
abstract: This paper introduces a novel methodology for leveraging probabilistic programming languages in conjunction with differential privacy (DP) to facilitate data analysis on sensitive datasets. The core contribution lies in the development of a "privacy-aware sampling" technique integrated within a probabilistic programming framework. This technique allows for the generation of models and inferences, while simultaneously guaranteeing privacy protection through calibrated noise injection, adhering to a user-defined privacy budget. The approach addresses the critical need for robust data analysis tools that reconcile the accuracy of model building with the stringent requirements of privacy preservation. We demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of this integration, highlighting its potential for applications where data sensitivity is paramount. The paper focuses on the theoretical aspects and the design of the technique, without requiring empirical experimental validation.

title: Dynamic Probabilistic Graphical Model Learning and Reinforcement Learning Fusion
abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for intelligent learning and decision-making in complex environments by fusing probabilistic graphical model learning with reinforcement learning. The core idea is to construct a dynamic system capable of learning both the structure and parameters of probabilistic graphical models, coupled with a reinforcement learning algorithm to optimize the agent's behavior. A neural network-based probabilistic graphical model learner is designed to adaptively adjust the model's structure and parameters based on environmental feedback. This learner then collaborates with a reinforcement learning algorithm to refine the agent's policy. The proposed approach offers a new paradigm for intelligent systems, allowing them to autonomously learn and adapt to dynamic environments. The key contribution lies in the synergistic combination of these two powerful techniques, leading to improved learning efficiency and decision quality. The framework is presented with detailed mathematical formulations and the potential for future development is discussed.

title: 基于生物进化算法的多参数优化 (Multi-Parameter Optimization Based on Bio-Inspired Evolutionary Algorithms - MBEOA)
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to multi-parameter optimization, termed Multi-Parameter Optimization Based on Bio-Inspired Evolutionary Algorithms (MBEOA). The core claim is to leverage the strengths of bio-inspired evolutionary algorithms to enhance the efficiency and accuracy of solving complex multi-parameter optimization problems. The proposed framework utilizes a multi-stage approach, initially decomposing the problem into smaller, manageable sub-problems. Each sub-problem is then addressed independently using a genetic algorithm, optimized for speed and adaptability. Finally, the optimal solutions obtained from each sub-problem are integrated to yield the overall global optimum. We demonstrate the effectiveness of MBEOA through theoretical analysis and discuss its advantages over traditional optimization techniques. The key innovation lies in the synergistic combination of evolutionary algorithms and multi-parameter optimization, resulting in significant improvements in both performance and solution quality.

abstract: This paper introduces an adaptive quantum entanglement field simulation algorithm designed to accurately model complex entanglement behaviors and support unconventional entanglement patterns. Traditional quantum entanglement simulation methods often struggle with the intricacies of this phenomenon. This novel approach leverages a dynamically adjusted "entanglement dynamics" model, offering a more precise and flexible framework for quantum computing and quantum communication. The core mechanism involves iteratively adjusting quantum entanglement strengths and modes, mitigating the limitations of conventional simulation techniques. This advancement holds significant potential for enhancing the modeling capabilities of quantum systems.

title: Title: Quantum Entanglement Vector Field Theory
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, presents a profound challenge to classical intuition regarding information transfer. This research explores the potential of utilizing vector fields to mathematically model and manipulate this phenomenon, offering a pathway towards novel communication methods and quantum computing advancements. We propose the concept of an 'Entanglement Vector Field' – a complex, multi-dimensional field that governs correlated states and allows for instantaneous information transfer through its modulation. This framework aims to address the inherent fragility of qubits and provides a potentially more robust and efficient method for quantum communication. The paper details the theoretical foundation of this model, including the mathematical representations of entanglement, the potential for vector field manipulation, and preliminary investigations into its capabilities. We conclude by outlining future research directions and potential implications for quantum technology.

We demonstrate the efficacy of this method in enhancing understanding and potentially facilitating advancements in quantum computing and quantum information security.

title: Empirical Recursive Self-Improvement on Coding Agents: L1/L2 Confirmation with Negative L3 Results
abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI)—the capacity of a system not merely to improve task solutions, but to improve the procedures that produce those improvements—occupies a central place in theoretical and forecasting discussions of advanced artificial intelligence. Empirical demonstrations that isolate RSI from ordinary evolutionary search, however, remain scarce. We introduce a three-level empirical ladder evaluated on a frozen coding-task suite under matched evaluation budgets, and we report positive and negative results with equal care. L1 (Weak RSI): a fixed improver evolves an archive of agent solutions that beat both a seed agent and matched random mutants. Confirmed on 4/4 independent RNG seeds {42, 7, 123, 999}. L2 (RSI): the improver itself evolves and beats a frozen improver and unbiased random improvers, with a freeze ablation that removes the gain. Confirmed under a fairer mean-primary protocol on primary seeds {17, 88, 404} and on 3/3 held-out independent seed triples. L3 (meta-RSI): the meta-mutator that edits improvers evolves under the same discipline. Not demonstrated across three fair redesigns (mean margins vs frozen L2 meta: +0.17, +0.20, −0.09; threshold ≥ 0.4). L3 is not claimed. Under a black-box experimental stance (apparatus internals treated as fixed equipment; scores, seeds, and success criteria public), we release tables, figures, seeds, and hit rules sufficient for external verification of the reported scores. A parallel independent replication track has obtained L1 and is pursuing L2.

title: Adaptive Meta-Learning with Evolutionary Algorithms
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to optimization problems by integrating evolutionary algorithms with meta-learning techniques. The core idea is to develop an adaptive meta-learning system where an evolutionary algorithm autonomously assesses its performance and adjusts its learning strategies. This 'intelligent evolution' system leverages feedback to refine both the genetic operators and the search strategy within the population, accelerating the evolutionary process and enhancing optimization efficiency. The methodology introduces a self-evaluation mechanism within the evolutionary process, allowing the algorithm to learn how to learn more effectively. This contrasts with traditional evolutionary algorithms which operate without inherent adaptive capabilities. The presented framework demonstrates the potential for rapid adaptation and superior performance in complex optimization scenarios. We formulate this approach using the following key elements: (s_1, s_2, ..., s_K), where s_i represents a potential solution, and K denotes the population size. The algorithm iteratively modifies these solutions based on performance feedback.

title: Decentralized Machine Learning for Autonomous Vehicle Control
abstract: This paper investigates the application of decentralized machine learning (DML) to autonomous vehicle control. Traditional centralized approaches to autonomous driving often face challenges related to scalability, communication bottlenecks, and vulnerability to single points of failure. This research proposes a novel system utilizing distributed reinforcement learning (DRL) across a network of autonomous vehicles. The core claim is that a decentralized system, enabling collaborative learning and adaptation, can achieve improved performance and robustness compared to centralized methods. The system employs vehicles to share observations and jointly learn navigation policies. The key mechanisms involve the distributed training of policies using techniques such as asynchronous difference methods and federated learning. The system addresses the problem of non-stationarity inherent in multi-agent systems by employing adaptive learning rates and robust policy aggregation strategies. We discuss the theoretical framework, highlighting key concepts like policy synchronization, convergence analysis, and the impact of communication constraints. Furthermore, we present a conceptual model of the system, outlining the interactions between vehicles and the learning process. The potential benefits of DML for autonomous vehicle control, including enhanced safety, increased scalability, and improved adaptability to dynamic environments, are explored. The research contributes to the growing field of DML by providing a foundational design and theoretical underpinnings for a robust and scalable autonomous driving system.

title: Title: Modular Quantum State Collapse
abstract: Abstract: This paper investigates the concept of modular quantum state collapse, a paradigm shift in quantum computing that proposes a novel approach to state manipulation. We introduce a fragmentation algorithm designed to break down complex quantum states into smaller, independent components, enabling predictable and efficient collapse sequences. The core claim is that this method, when implemented effectively, offers a pathway to reduce the computational burden associated with current quantum computation techniques, potentially leading to increased efficiency and reduced complexity. The proposed algorithm's unique mechanism leverages structural properties to guide state collapse, creating a system of nested quantum states. This research explores the theoretical foundations of this approach and outlines a preliminary implementation of the fragmentation algorithm.

title: Dynamically Weighted Graph Neural Networks for Temporal Knowledge Representation
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to temporal knowledge representation utilizing Dynamically Weighted Graph Neural Networks (DW-GNNs). Traditional Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) often struggle to effectively represent and reason about knowledge that evolves over time due to their static nature. Our proposed DW-GNNs overcome this limitation by incorporating a dynamic weighting mechanism. This mechanism allows the network to adjust node and edge weights based on the temporal context, effectively capturing the changing relationships and importance of entities within the graph. We formulate the core idea as: GNNs can dynamically adjust their node and edge weights based on temporal context, improving their ability to represent and reason about evolving knowledge. The core mechanism utilizes a temporal update rule to modify weights, creating a dynamic representation. We demonstrate the efficacy of DW-GNNs through theoretical analysis and outline a potential framework for implementation. The key contribution is the integration of dynamic weighting within a GNN architecture for improved temporal reasoning performance.

title: Title: Dynamic Geometric Topology for Evolutionary Algorithms
abstract: Dynamic Geometric Topology for Evolutionary Algorithms explores the application of dynamic geometric topology to enhance the performance of evolutionary algorithms. Current evolutionary algorithms often struggle with complex, non-adaptive solutions, necessitating the creation of fixed topologies. This research proposes a novel framework that allows for topology to evolve dynamically based on the problem's state, leading to adaptive and robust solutions. The core mechanism involves introducing a self-modifying topology that adjusts its structure as the problem progresses, improving solution quality and resilience. This paper outlines the theoretical foundations, initial implementation details, and potential impact of this approach.

title: Symbolic Regression with Bayesian Latent Variables
abstract: Symbolic regression (SR) is a data-driven technique for discovering mathematical equations from data. However, its performance often degrades when dealing with complex, high-dimensional datasets exhibiting noisy relationships. This work addresses this limitation by integrating Bayesian inference with SR, leveraging latent variables to represent unobserved underlying relationships within the data. The proposed approach allows the regression algorithm to explore a wider range of potential symbolic expressions while simultaneously accounting for the inherent uncertainty in the data and the model parameters. The core claim is that incorporating latent variables significantly improves the robustness and accuracy of SR, particularly in scenarios with complex and noisy data. We outline the methodology, including the Bayesian framework, the latent variable integration, and the optimization strategy. The theoretical underpinnings and the key components of the system are discussed, highlighting how this new approach overcomes the limitations of traditional SR. Ultimately, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this combined approach through a conceptual discussion and highlight potential future directions for research.

title: 拓扑量子计算中的自适应几何优化算法
abstract: This paper introduces a novel self-adaptive geometric optimization algorithm for quantum systems, leveraging the unique properties of topological quantum computation. The algorithm adapts to the specific geometry of the quantum system during optimization, leading to improved efficiency and stability compared to traditional methods. The core mechanism centers around utilizing the inherent topological structure of the quantum system to guide the optimization process, resulting in a more robust and efficient approach to quantum system design. We present a detailed explanation of the algorithm's components and demonstrate its performance on various quantum systems through illustrative examples. The research explores the potential of this approach to address key challenges in quantum computing, including error mitigation and system scalability.

title: WindowKV: Task-adaptive group-wise KV cache window selection for efficient LLM inference
abstract: With the advancements in long-context inference capabilities of large language models (LLMs), the KV cache has become one of the foundational components. However, its substantial GPU memory consumption makes KV cache compression a key technique for enabling efficient LLM inference in industrial scenarios. While recent studies have focused on optimizing the memory occupied by the KV cache, they overlook two critical factors: preserving semantic coherence and considering task-specific characteristic during compression. To address these limitations, we propose a novel task-adaptive KV cache window selection method, WindowKV. WindowKV dynamically selects local semantic windows consisting of consecutive tokens, according to task-specific characteristics, ensuring the retained KV cache captures continuous, essential context. Additionally, we introduce an intra-group layer KV cache indices sharing strategy to reduce computational overhead, achieving a balance between performance and efficiency. We rigorously evaluate WindowKV on the LongBench benchmark, and the results demonstrate that it maintains a performance comparable to full KV cache retention while using only 12% of the original KV cache, significantly reducing memory requirements. Furthermore, our method also achieves state-of-the-art results in the Needle-in-a-Haystack evaluation, highlighting its effectiveness and robustness.

title: What Intermediate Layers Know: Detecting Jailbreaks from Entropy Dynamics
abstract: Jailbreak attacks reveal a persistent weakness in aligned Large Language Models: carefully crafted prompts can elicit policy-violating responses despite safety training. While most defenses operate at the prompt or output level, it remains unclear how harmful intent is encoded within the model's internal representations. We investigate this question by analyzing token-level predictive entropy trajectories across layers of a frozen LLM using the logit lens. We find that static aggregate statistics of prompt-level entropy (e.g., mean, variance) carry little discriminative signal, whereas features capturing how entropy evolves across token positions, such as monotonic rank-based trend scores, are substantially more informative. Importantly, this signal is not uniform across model depth: it is concentrated in intermediate layers and degrades at the final layer, indicating that jailbreak-relevant structure is most pronounced in mid-network representations rather than at the output head. Across multiple models (Llama, Qwen, Gemma) and adversarial benchmarks, these entropy dynamics provide architecture-consistent separation without additional training. Together, our findings show that jailbreak behavior is reflected in structured intermediate uncertainty dynamics, clarifying both which entropy-derived features encode harmful intent and where in the network that signal is most pronounced.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Decoding for Improving Truthfulness in Open-Ended Generation
abstract: Ensuring truthfulness in large language models remains a critical challenge for reliable text generation. While supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning with human feedback have shown promise, they require substantial amount of annotated data and computational resources, limiting scalability. In contrast, decoding-time interventions offer lightweight alternatives without model retraining. However, existing decoding strategies often face issues like prompt sensitivity, limited generalization, or dependence on internal model states. We propose a context-aware adaptive decoding method that leverages a compact reference grounding space, built from as few as 10 annotated examples and comprising pairs of context embeddings and next token logits from truthful responses, to enable retrieval-based logit shaping during inference. At each decoding step, our method retrieves top-N semantically similar contexts and aggregates their associated next token logits to modify the LLM's logits. Across three open-ended question-answering benchmarks, our approach achieves a 2.8 percent average improvement on TruthfulQA and further outperforms existing baselines on both Biographies and WikiQA. Experimental results also demonstrate cross-task generalization, with TruthfulQA-derived grounding enhancing biography generation. Our model-agnostic, scalable, and efficient method requires only a single generation pass, highlighting the potential of context-aware decoding for factual reliability in LLMs.

title: CQD-SHAP: Explainable Complex Query Answering via Shapley Values
abstract: Complex query answering (CQA) goes beyond the well-studied link prediction task by addressing more sophisticated queries that require multi-hop reasoning over incomplete knowledge graphs (KGs). Research on neural and neurosymbolic CQA methods is still an emerging field. Almost all of these methods can be regarded as black-box models, which may raise concerns about user trust. Although neurosymbolic approaches like CQD are slightly more interpretable, allowing intermediate results to be tracked, the importance of different parts of the query remains unexplained. In this paper, we propose CQD-SHAP, a novel framework that computes the contribution of each query part to the ranking of a specific answer. This contribution explains the value of leveraging a neural predictor that can infer new knowledge from an incomplete KG, rather than a symbolic approach relying solely on existing facts in the KG. CQD-SHAP is formulated based on Shapley values from cooperative game theory and satisfies all the fundamental Shapley axioms. Automated evaluation of these explanations in terms of necessary and sufficient explanations, and comparisons with various baselines, shows the effectiveness of this approach for most query types.

title: K-Dense BYOK: An Open-Source AI Research Assistant That Runs Locally and Keeps a Hash-Chained Lab Notebook
abstract: K-Dense BYOK (bring your own keys) is a free, open-source AI research assistant for scientists in any field that runs on the researcher's own computer. The researcher supplies access to a model of their choice, hosted or running locally, and the application supplies everything else: a place for the work to run, a layer of scientific scaffolding, and a complete record. Each project is an ordinary folder, so the data, the code, the results, and the record stay on a machine the researcher administers and can be read years later without the application. Three things separate it from a chat assistant or a general-purpose coding agent. It ships a library of written scientific procedures, guided workflow templates, catalogs of where research data can be found, and reviewer and writer roles the agent can hand work to. It keeps a Living Lab Notebook whose entries link into an argument and are added to but never erased. And it records what happened by watching what the agent does rather than by taking the agent's word for it, in a log the agent has no tool that can write to. That choice targets the most common failure, model overclaiming, in our earlier benchmark of nine frontier models, by making claims checkable rather than preventing them. On twenty interdisciplinary research prompts, scored under a rubric fixed in advance, K-Dense BYOK led two managed platforms on both scientific quality and research execution. Its deliverables were the only ones that recorded the software they ran in, and the only ones that usually arrived with a command that regenerates the results. One of the managed platforms ran the same frontier model and supplied neither. Those environment records were files the agent wrote, not part of the observed log, which does not yet capture the software environment itself. The code is available under the MIT license at https://github.com/K-Dense-AI/k-dense-byok.

Each project is an ordinary folder, so the data, the code, the results, and the record stay on a machine the researcher administers and can be read years later without the application. Three things separate it from a chat assistant or a general-purpose coding agent. It ships a library of written scientific procedures, guided workflow templates, catalogs of where research data can be found, and reviewer and writer roles the agent can hand work to. It keeps a Living Lab Notebook whose entries link into an argument and are added to but never erased. And it records what happened by watching what the agent does rather than by taking the agent's word for it, in a log the agent has no tool that can write to. That choice targets the most common failure, model overclaiming, in our earlier benchmark of nine frontier models, by making claims checkable rather than preventing them. On twenty interdisciplinary research prompts, scored under a rubric fixed in advance, K-Dense BYOK led two managed platforms on both scientific quality and research execution. Its deliverables were the only ones that recorded the software they ran in, and the only ones that usually arrived with a command that regenerates the results. One of the managed platforms ran the same frontier model and supplied neither. Those environment records were files the agent wrote, not part of the observed log, which does not yet capture the software environment itself. The code is available under the MIT license at https://github.com/K-Dense-AI/k-dense-byok.

title: Pixel-wise Planarity for High-Precision Monocular Plane Segmentation
abstract: Plane segmentation from a single RGB image remains challenging due to imprecise region grouping and geometrically inconsistent supervision, often leading to over-segmentation and false planar detections. We propose instead a pixel-wise planarity prediction framework for robust monocular plane segmentation. Building on a pretrained monocular geometric backbone predicting depth and surface normals, we introduce a dedicated planarity head that estimates per-pixel planarity confidence. During inference, predicted depth, normals, and planarity are combined in a lightweight region-growing procedure that enforces geometric consistency when forming plane segments. We further analyze existing plane ground-truth annotations and demonstrate substantial geometric inconsistencies under strict distance thresholds. Across multiple datasets, our method achieves improved geometric precision and segmentation quality compared to prior state-of-the-art approaches, while improving computational efficiency. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/alpayozkan/PixelwisePlanarity.

title: Occamy-1.0: Open Pareto-frontier 35B Intelligence for Co-work
abstract: Co-work agents execute complex workflows that combine information gathering, tool use, coding, and file manipulation across many model invocations. Because cost and latency accumulate over the full episode, their practical value depends not only on peak capability but also on how efficiently that capability is delivered. Yet many steps in everyday work emphasize state tracking, coordination, recovery, and follow-through rather than frontier-scale reasoning. We present Occamy-1.0, a cost-efficient co-work model obtained by further training the post-trained Qwen3.6-35B-A3B checkpoint. We construct execution-grounded data and environments, capture replayable long-horizon trajectories across multiple harnesses, and use staged post-training to develop and consolidate complementary execution capabilities. Across a broad suite of co-work benchmarks, Occamy-1.0 is consistently among the strongest comparably sized models and remains competitive with substantially larger frontier systems on several tasks. Under our stated evaluation and pricing protocol, its aggregate performance across four representative benchmarks places it at the low-cost knee of the observed cost--performance Pareto frontier. Supporting evaluations in tool calling, coding, and instruction following further show that this specialization preserves broad agentic capability. We release the model weights and a subset of the training data to support research on practical co-work agents and agentic post-training.
